new.title: Browse 30,000 objects at the Deutsches Ledermuseum
new.desc: Offenbach was once Germany's leather goods capital, and this museum was founded in 1917 by the architect Hugo Eberhardt as a teaching collection for young craftsmen. Today it holds more than 30,000 objects from many cultures and eras, from luxury bags and fashion to everyday tools and ethnological pieces.
new.tip: Plan a good hour and keep an eye out for the shoe galleries. It is a short walk from the S-Bahn stop Offenbach Marktplatz.
new.q: Deutsches Ledermuseum, Frankfurter Straße 86, Offenbach am Main

new.title: Find the Renaissance arcades of the Isenburger Schloss
new.desc: The counts of Isenburg built this palace on the Main in the 16th century. Its two faces could hardly be more different: the town side is an airy Renaissance facade with arcades between two stair towers, while the river side keeps the fortress-like walls of an older castle. A four-wing palace was planned but never finished.
new.tip: Walk round to compare both facades, then carry on along the Offenbach riverbank, which is lovely at sunset.
new.q: Isenburger Schloss, Schloßstraße, Offenbach am Main

new.title: Visit Einhard's basilica in Seligenstadt
new.desc: The church of St. Marcellinus and Petrus goes back to Einhard, the courtier and biographer of Charlemagne, who founded a monastery here in the 9th century. Locals still call it the Einhard basilica, and it remained the abbey church until secularisation turned it into the parish church.
new.tip: Behind the church the former Benedictine abbey has restored baroque gardens that are a quiet spot for a stroll. The old town's half-timbered market square is two minutes away.

new.title: Drink a Hessian beer at Glaabsbräu in Seligenstadt
new.desc: Founded in 1744 and still run by the Glaab family, Glaabsbräu calls itself the oldest brewery in southern Hesse. The brewery on Frankfurter Straße offers guided tours with tastings, and its beers are poured in pubs all over Seligenstadt's old town.
new.tip: Book a brewery tour on their website in advance. Afterwards, try a Glaabsbräu in one of the taverns around the Marktplatz.

new.title: Swim in the Langener Waldsee
new.desc: Covering 89 hectares, this lake in the woods south of Frankfurt is the largest bathing lake and the biggest body of water in the whole Rhine-Main area. A lido with sandy beaches and lawns stretches along the shore.
new.tip: The lido charges admission and fills up fast on hot weekends, so go on a weekday or early in the morning.

new.title: Wander from dinosaurs to Beuys at the Landesmuseum
new.desc: The Hessisches Landesmuseum is one of the oldest public museums in Germany and a true universal museum, covering art, cultural history and natural history under one roof. After years of renovation the main building on Friedensplatz reopened in 2014.
new.tip: Do not miss the Block Beuys, the largest work complex by Joseph Beuys kept in its original arrangement.

new.title: Spot the trees on the roof of the Waldspirale
new.desc: Friedensreich Hundertwasser designed this housing block in Darmstadt, completed in 2000. It spirals upwards like a horseshoe, with a roof planted with trees, onion domes and windows that are all different.
new.tip: It is a private residential building, so admire it from the street and the inner courtyard and keep your voice down.

new.title: Read in the painted garden house of the Prinz-Georg-Garten
new.desc: This formal garden in the French style has been laid out since 1698 and still has its geometric beds, basins and sundials. Its little Prettlack garden house of around 1711 is painted inside and out with trees and garlands and today holds a small reading library. The palais next door houses the grand-ducal porcelain collection.
new.tip: Come on a summer afternoon, borrow a book from the garden house and find a bench among the flowerbeds.

new.title: Smell 200 kinds of roses on the Rosenhöhe
new.desc: Princess Wilhelmine of Baden turned a former vineyard into this landscape park around 1810. Around 1900 Grand Duke Ernst Ludwig added the terraced rose garden at the top, where more than 200 varieties bloom from June into autumn, and in 1927 the Löwentor gate with its six lions by Bernhard Hoetger.
new.tip: Enter through the Löwentor and look for the two grand-ducal mausoleums in the trees. The Mathildenhöhe is a short walk away.

new.title: See the hunting lodge at Kranichstein
new.desc: Landgrave Georg I built this lodge in the north of Darmstadt between 1578 and 1580, and it later became a summer residence of the landgraves. It is one of the few surviving baroque hunting courts in Germany and now houses a hunting museum, the bioversum nature museum and a hotel with a restaurant.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk in the surrounding Kranichstein forest, and kids will enjoy the hands-on bioversum.

new.title: Take a dip in the Großer Woog
new.desc: Darmstadt has a natural bathing lake right on the eastern edge of its city centre. The Woog, as everyone calls it, has a lido with lawns that has been a summer meeting place for generations of Darmstadt locals.
new.tip: Come in the early evening, when the crowds thin out and the light over the water turns golden.

new.title: Join the crowds at the Heinerfest
new.desc: With about 250 showmen and some 700,000 visitors, Darmstadt's Heinerfest is one of the biggest inner-city festivals in Germany. Every year in early July, rides, stages and food stalls fill the streets around the palace.
new.tip: Go on a weekday evening for a slightly calmer crowd, and come hungry.

new.title: Shop the market Darmstadt has held since 1330
new.desc: Darmstadt has held a market on its oldest square, the Marktplatz in front of the Renaissance town hall, since 1330. On Wednesdays and Saturdays more than 60 stalls sell regional fruit, vegetables, cheese, bread and meat.
new.tip: Saturday morning is the liveliest time. Grab a sausage and sit by the old market fountain, which once supplied the town's water.

new.title: Drink house-brewed beer in the Darmstädter Ratskeller
new.desc: The Renaissance Old Town Hall on the south side of the Marktplatz hides a small brewery that has been making its own beer here since 1989. The Ratskeller serves it fresh with hearty home-style food, inside or on the square in front of the palace.
new.tip: Ask for the seasonal beer, and on market days take a table outside to watch the stalls.

new.title: Have a beer at the Braustüb'l by the station
new.desc: The Darmstadt tourist board calls the Braustüb'l the mother of all pubs. It has stood next to the main station since 1880 and is the tap room of the Darmstädter Privatbrauerei, which brews under the Braustüb'l name.
new.tip: Ideal while waiting for a train. In summer the outdoor tables are the place to be.

new.title: Taste a fresh Grohe at the brewery tap
new.desc: Grohe is Darmstadt's other old brewery, and its tap house on Nieder-Ramstädter Straße pours its beer straight from the brewery with regional and seasonal dishes. Locals treat the place and its outdoor seating as a meeting point.
new.tip: Try the Grohe Hell with a schnitzel, and reserve a table on weekend evenings.

new.title: Hike up to Burg Frankenstein
new.desc: The ruined castle of Frankenstein crowns a hill above Mühltal and the Bergstraße, with views across the Rhine plain on clear days. The name and its spooky associations have made it famous for its Halloween events every autumn.
new.tip: Walk up through the forest from Nieder-Beerbach for the best approach. Avoid the Halloween weekends unless you have a ticket, as the road gets very busy.

new.title: Climb up to the Veste Otzberg
new.desc: This fortress sits on the 368 metre summit of the Otzberg, an old volcanic cone at the northern edge of the Odenwald. The village of Hering grew from the castle's outer bailey, and the round keep looks out over the hills of Darmstadt-Dieburg.
new.tip: Climb the keep for the view, then stroll through Hering's half-timbered lanes on the way back down.

new.title: Taste Odenwald wine at vinum autmundis
new.desc: Groß-Umstadt is the heart of a small wine island on the edge of the Odenwald. Its cooperative vinum autmundis is the largest wine producer around, with about 100 members working some 75 hectares.
new.tip: Stop by the wine shop to taste before you buy. In September the town celebrates its wine at the Umstädter Winzerfest on the market square.

new.title: Explore the huge ruin of Burg Königstein
new.desc: The fortress ruin above Königstein is the town's landmark and one of the largest castle ruins in Germany. You can roam its walls, cellars and towers and look out over the Taunus to the Frankfurt skyline.
new.tip: Afterwards, walk down to the Hauptstraße for cake in one of the cafés.

new.title: Eat Austrian-style cake at Café Kreiner
new.desc: Café-Konditorei Kreiner on Königstein's Hauptstraße is famous across the region for cakes and pastries in the old Austrian tradition. The interior has kept its 1970s look with great care, which only adds to the charm.
new.tip: It closes in the late afternoon, so come after a morning walk in the Taunus.
new.q: Café Kreiner, Hauptstraße 10, Königstein im Taunus

new.title: Look out from the keep of Burg Kronberg
new.desc: Kronberg's castle combines a Staufer-era upper castle with a striking free-standing keep, a late medieval chapel and a later middle castle that locals simply called the Schloss. It rises above the half-timbered lanes of the old town.
new.tip: Wander down through the Kronberg old town afterwards; the lanes below the castle are among the prettiest in the Taunus.

new.title: Spend a day at the Opel-Zoo
new.desc: Georg von Opel founded this zoo on the slopes of the Taunus in 1956 as a research enclosure. Today about 1,700 animals of 200 species live here, and with some 580,000 visitors a year it is one of the most visited attractions in Hesse. It runs entirely on tickets and donations.
new.tip: The zoo sits right at the foot of the Altkönig, so you can combine it with a hike. Buses run from Kronberg station.
new.q: Opel-Zoo, Königsteiner Straße 35, Kronberg im Taunus

new.title: Hike to the Celtic ring walls on the Altkönig
new.desc: At 798 metres the Altkönig is the third highest summit of the Taunus. Its top is ringed by the stone walls of a Celtic hillfort, and the spurs below hold old viewpoints such as the Viktoriatempel.
new.tip: Bring water and sturdy shoes, as the summit is rocky and has no restaurant. The inns at the Fuchstanz saddle make a good stop on the way.

new.title: Tour the landgraves' palace in Bad Homburg
new.desc: From 1622 Bad Homburg's palace was the residence of the landgraves of Hessen-Homburg, and after 1866 the summer home of the Prussian kings and German emperors. The tall White Tower in the courtyard survives from the medieval castle.
new.tip: The palace park is free to walk around. Join a guided tour to see the emperor's rooms.
new.q: Schloss Bad Homburg, Bad Homburg vor der Höhe

new.title: Join the lantern parade at the Laternenfest
new.desc: Bad Homburg's Laternenfest was first held in 1935 and takes place every year on the fifth weekend after 1 August, usually the end of August or start of September. For four days the town fills with lanterns, rides and stalls, topped by a big parade.
new.tip: The big lantern parade is the highlight, so stake out a spot along the route early.
new.q: Louisenstraße, Bad Homburg vor der Höhe

new.title: Eat in the beer garden of the Alt Oberurseler Brauhaus
new.desc: In a baroque house in Oberursel's old town, the Alt Oberurseler Brauhaus brews its own beer and serves hearty home-style food. In summer the beer garden is packed with locals.
new.tip: Ask for the house beer from the tank, and take a short walk through the old town lanes around the Marktplatz afterwards.

new.title: Walk through the imperial castle of Friedberg
new.desc: Founded around 1171 to 1180, probably under Frederick Barbarossa, Friedberg's imperial castle covers about 3.9 hectares and is one of the largest castle complexes in Germany. Its landmark is the Adolfsturm, a mid 14th-century tower over 54 metres tall.
new.tip: The castle grounds are free to wander. On weekend afternoons the history society opens the Adolfsturm, with viewing platforms high over the Wetterau.

new.title: Descend into Friedberg's medieval Jewish bath
new.desc: Friedberg's mikveh is the largest completely preserved medieval ritual bath in Germany. A stone staircase leads deep underground to the water at the bottom of the shaft.
new.tip: It is only a few steps from the Kaiserstraße. Check the opening hours, which are limited.

new.title: Breathe the salty air at Bad Nauheim's graduation towers
new.desc: Bad Nauheim still has five graduation towers, long walls of brushwood over which brine trickles to leave a salty mist in the air. Most of them can be visited freely, and a windmill tower stands between two of them along the so-called Long Wall.
new.tip: Walk the length slowly and breathe deeply; locals come here like to a seaside promenade.

new.title: Follow Elvis Presley around Bad Nauheim
new.desc: Elvis Presley was stationed in nearby Friedberg as a soldier and lived in Bad Nauheim from 1958 to 1960, from 1959 in a house at Goethestraße 14. The town has not forgotten: a pedestrian light shows Elvis with his guitar on green.
new.tip: Look out for the Burgscheune archway, which appeared on the cover of the single A Big Hunk o' Love.

new.title: Climb the Wetterau inkpot at Burg Münzenberg
new.desc: Locals call the ruin of Burg Münzenberg the Wetterau inkpot because of its two round towers. Known since 1162, it is one of the most important high medieval castles in Germany and stands on a hill visible from far across the plain.
new.tip: Climb one of the towers for a view over the whole Wetterau, and come in the late afternoon for the best light.

new.title: Meet the Celtic prince at the Glauberg
new.desc: The Keltenwelt am Glauberg is an archaeology museum built beside a reconstructed Celtic burial mound. At the centre of its exhibition stands the Celtic prince of the Glauberg, a life-size stone statue found here.
new.tip: Walk up to the plateau above the museum for the archaeological park and the views.

new.title: Shop the Hanau market under the Brothers Grimm
new.desc: On Wednesdays and Saturdays Hanau's weekly market fills the Marktplatz in front of the town hall. Watching over the stalls is the national monument to Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, who were born in Hanau.
new.tip: Go before noon, as the stalls pack up early in the afternoon. Fresh produce from the Wetterau and Main valley is the thing to buy.

new.title: Visit Schloss Philippsruhe on the Main
new.desc: Count Philipp Reinhard of Hanau built this baroque palace on the Main between about 1700 and 1725. Its interiors were remodelled in the 1880s and now hold the Historical Museum of Hanau.
new.tip: Walk through the park down to the river, where the view of the palace is best.

new.title: Stroll the old spa park of Wilhelmsbad
new.desc: Wilhelmsbad was laid out as a spa in the 1770s and is surrounded by a large English landscape park with an artificial castle ruin. The Comoedienhaus theatre dates from 1781, and the old Kurhaus houses the Hessian doll and toy museum.
new.tip: Bring a picnic and look for the old carousel pavilion on its little hill.

new.title: Visit the Grimms' childhood home in Steinau
new.desc: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm spent their childhood from 1791 to 1796 in the Amtshaus of Steinau an der Straße, a building from 1562. It is now a museum about the brothers and their fairy tales.
new.tip: Next door is Schloss Steinau, one of the best-preserved early Renaissance palaces in Hesse, so plan time for both.
new.q: Brüder Grimm-Haus, Steinau an der Straße

new.title: Climb the keep of the Ronneburg
new.desc: The Ronneburg stands on a basalt cone east of Frankfurt and dates back to the 13th century. Its 32 metre keep with a Renaissance dome has telescopes at the top, and the castle has a well about 96 metres deep. In 1736 Count Zinzendorf and the Moravian Brethren found refuge here.
new.tip: Look out for the knights' tournaments and medieval markets that a friends' association holds at the castle.

new.title: Step into a Roman villa at the Pompejanum
new.desc: King Ludwig I of Bavaria had this copy of a house from Pompeii, the Casa dei Dioscuri, built on the high bank of the Main in Aschaffenburg. Its painted rooms show how a wealthy Roman family lived.
new.tip: It is only open in the warmer months. Walk back along the river terraces to Schloss Johannisburg.

new.title: Find Grünewald's painting in the Stiftsbasilika
new.desc: The collegiate church of St. Peter and Alexander is Aschaffenburg's oldest church, with Romanesque roots and a rich art collection. Its most famous treasure is the Lamentation of Christ by Matthias Grünewald.
new.tip: Look for the Romanesque cloister on the side, and the Stiftsmuseum next door for more art.
new.q: Stiftsbasilika St. Peter und Alexander, Aschaffenburg

new.title: Stroll the English garden of Park Schönbusch
new.desc: Across the Main from the palace, Park Schönbusch is one of the oldest and largest English landscape gardens in Germany. Its little pavilions, bridges and lakes make it the city's favourite place for a Sunday walk.
new.tip: Walk there from the old town across the Main, and look for the view axis that lines up the park with Schloss Johannisburg.

new.title: See the fairy-tale water castle of Mespelbrunn
new.desc: Hidden in a side valley of the Spessart, Schloss Mespelbrunn has belonged to the same family since the early 15th century. Its reflection in the moat has made it one of the most photographed castles in Germany, and it starred in the 1958 film Das Wirtshaus im Spessart.
new.tip: Come early to beat the tour buses. Guided tours run in season, and the forest walks around it are lovely.

new.title: Drink Franconian wine at Hofgut Hörstein
new.desc: Alzenau is the smallest of Franconia's wine areas, with about 90 hectares of vines in Hörstein, Wasserlos and Michelbach, where monks planted the first vines around the year 1000. The Hofgut Hörstein serves its wines with local food.
new.tip: Walk the seven kilometre Kulturweg Wein und Herrschaft through the vineyards first, which starts here. The Hofgut is closed on Mondays.

new.title: Admire the half-timbered Schnatterloch
new.desc: Miltenberg's sloping market square, called the Schnatterloch, is lined with richly carved half-timbered houses and has a Renaissance fountain in the middle. The Mildenburg rises above it on the wooded hill.
new.tip: Take the steps up from the square to the castle for the view back over the roofs.

new.title: Look over the Main from the Mildenburg
new.desc: The Mildenburg was built in the mid 12th century above Miltenberg and later belonged to the archbishops of Mainz. Its keep gives a view along the bend of the Main and over the red sandstone roofs below.
new.tip: Climb the keep, and check what is on in the castle museum before you go.

new.title: Eat regional food at the Faust Braustuben
new.desc: Brauhaus Faust in Miltenberg's Schwarzviertel goes back to the Löwenbrauerei of the 17th century and is run by the fourth generation of the Faust family. It was named German brewery of the year in 2018. Its Braustuben serve the beers with Franconian food.
new.tip: Sit in the beer garden in summer, and ask about the brewing courses if you want to try making your own beer.

new.title: Climb to the monastery tavern at Kloster Engelberg
new.desc: Above Großheubach, the Franciscan monastery of Engelberg sits on a hill over the Main valley. Pilgrims and walkers climb the long staircase of red sandstone steps through the vineyards, then rest in the Klosterschänke with a view across to Miltenberg.
new.tip: The tavern is closed on Mondays. Walk up the steps from Großheubach rather than driving.

new.title: Taste red wine from sandstone at Weingut Fürst
new.desc: The Fürst family estate in Bürgstadt is one of Germany's best known producers of Pinot Noir, grown on steep red sandstone terraces such as the Klingenberger Schlossberg. It is a member of the VDP and has been named winery of the year.
new.tip: Phone ahead before visiting the wine shop, as opening hours are limited, especially on Saturdays.

new.title: Hear the Stumm organ in Amorbach
new.desc: The former Benedictine abbey church of Amorbach holds an organ completed by the Stumm brothers in 1782. Enlarged in 1982, it now has 66 stops and about 5,100 pipes. The abbey's classicist Green Hall is another highlight.
new.tip: Join a guided tour of the abbey, and check the schedule for organ recitals, mostly held in the summer months.

new.title: Wander the oldest botanical garden still in place
new.desc: Gießen's botanical garden was founded in 1609 and is the oldest north of the Alps still at its original site. About 8,000 plant species grow here, most labelled in German and Latin.
new.tip: It is right next to the old town and free, perfect for a break between sights.

new.title: See Justus Liebig's laboratory
new.desc: The chemist Justus Liebig lived and worked in this building from 1824 to 1852, and his laboratory has been preserved as it was. The museum, founded in 1920, is counted among the most important chemistry museums in the world.
new.tip: Take the guided tour if you can, as it brings the old benches and apparatus to life.

new.title: Have a beer in Gießen's oldest student cellar
new.desc: The Scarabée on Riegelpfad has been a cult pub since 1962 and calls itself the oldest student cellar in Gießen. Generations of students have drunk, argued and danced in its vaults.
new.tip: It only really gets going late in the evening, so make it your last stop of the night.

new.title: Walk among the ruins of Kloster Arnsburg
new.desc: Cistercian monks founded Arnsburg near Lich in 1174. After the abbey was dissolved, its late Romanesque and early Gothic church was left roofless, and its arches now stand open to the sky.
new.tip: It is a peaceful place for a walk. Lich, home of the Licher brewery, is a short drive away.

new.title: Stand at Elisabeth's tomb in the Elisabethkirche
new.desc: Begun in 1235 over the grave of St. Elisabeth of Thuringia, this is considered the oldest purely Gothic church in Germany. In the late Middle Ages it was one of the great pilgrimage sites of Europe.
new.tip: Pay the small fee to see the golden shrine of St. Elisabeth in the choir area.

new.title: Watch the rooster on Marburg's town hall
new.desc: Marburg's late Gothic town hall was built between 1512 and 1527 on the market square of the upper town. Every hour a copper rooster at the top of its gable flaps its wings.
new.tip: Be on the square just before the hour. The cafés around it are ideal for waiting.

new.title: Have breakfast at Café Barfuß
new.desc: Café Barfuß sits on the Barfüßerstraße, the main lane of Marburg's upper town, and has long been a favourite of students. It is best known for its generous breakfasts.
new.tip: Breakfast is served until early afternoon, so it is perfect for a late start.

new.title: Sip wine at the Weinlädele on the castle steps
new.desc: The Weinlädele sits on the Schlosstreppe, the steps between the market square and the castle. For decades it served nothing but wine, and today it adds hearty regional dishes; its cheese plate is a classic.
new.tip: Get there early for a seat outside on the steps.

new.title: Climb the Spiegelslustturm above Marburg
new.desc: The Kaiser-Wilhelm-Turm, which everyone calls the Spiegelslustturm, was built from 1887 to 1890 on the Lahnberge hills. Its 167 steps lead 36 metres up to a view straight across the valley to the castle and the Elisabethkirche.
new.tip: Walk up from the Elisabethkirche through the forest; the view is best in the late afternoon.

new.title: Walk up the volcano town of Amöneburg
new.desc: The small town of Amöneburg sits on top of a 365 metre basalt hill, the northernmost outcrop of the Vogelsberg volcanic field. A castle ruin crowns the summit and the views over the flat Amöneburg basin are huge.
new.tip: Walk around the edge of the hill at sunset, when the whole basin glows below you.

new.title: Cross Wetzlar's old Lahn bridge
new.desc: Wetzlar's stone bridge over the Lahn was probably built in the 13th century and has seven arches. It is one of the oldest surviving bridges in Hesse and leads straight up into the old town.
new.tip: Stand on the riverbank downstream for the classic view of the bridge with the Dom behind it.

new.title: Visit the Lottehaus of Goethe's Werther
new.desc: Charlotte Buff was born in this 1653 half-timbered house in 1753. Goethe fell for her during his time in Wetzlar and turned her into Lotte in The Sorrows of Young Werther. The house is now a museum.
new.tip: Pair it with a walk through the old town to the Jerusalem House, linked to the other side of the Werther story.

new.title: Tour the fairy-tale Schloss Braunfels
new.desc: Since the 13th century this castle on a basalt hill has been the seat of the counts of Solms, and it is still owned by the family. Its towers and turrets date mostly from a romantic neo-Gothic rebuild of the late 19th century.
new.tip: Join a guided tour of the interiors, then have a coffee in the little market square below the castle.

new.title: See the world's largest candle in Schlitz
new.desc: Schlitz is a little town of five castles, with the Hinterburg and its tall Hinterturm at the centre. Every Advent the tower is dressed up as a giant candle, lit with a flame at the top, and the town calls it the largest candle in the world.
new.tip: Come on an evening in December when the flame is lit and the old town is at its most atmospheric.

new.title: Taste German whisky at the Schlitzer Destillerie
new.desc: The Schlitzer Korn- und Edelobstbrennerei in Schlitz distils korn, fruit brandies and German whisky. Open days and whisky events give a look behind the scenes of the stills.
new.tip: Check the shop hours before you come, and ask to taste the whisky alongside the fruit brandies.

new.title: Cycle the Vulkanradweg into the Vogelsberg
new.desc: The Vulkanradweg follows old railway lines for 94 kilometres from the Wetterau up into the high Vogelsberg, a vast extinct volcano. The gentle gradients make it easy going despite the climb.
new.tip: Plan two days for the whole route or pick a stretch; the old station buildings along the way make good rest stops.
